one_liner: CNCF Go messaging server whose built-in JetStream persistence showed ~14x lower median latency than Kafka at light load.
what_it_does: JetStream is the persistence layer built into nats-server, a single Go binary that you turn on with `-js`. Streams capture messages published on NATS subjects into file (the default) or memory storage, with limits, interest or work-queue retention. Consumers (pull or push, durable or ephemeral) replay by sequence or time and track per-message acks, and streams can be replicated R1-R5 over Raft; the KV and Object Store APIs are built on top. It does not speak the Kafka protocol: you use NATS clients (40+ languages) and subject-based addressing instead of topics, partitions and offsets.
how_it_is_fast: In this test the gap is mostly per-message path length and client defaults, not a storage algorithm: nats.go flushes each publish as soon as its flusher goroutine is kicked (no linger timer), while franz-go defaults to a 10 ms producer linger. On the server, the file store appends each record with a HighwayHash-64 checksum into a write-through cache of the current message block and, for unreplicated streams, writes it straight to the OS ("flush in place"), with fsync only every 2 minutes by default. A signal goroutine then matches the subject against the stream's consumer sublist and wakes the consumer loop, which serves the waiting pull request from that cache. Per-subject state is kept in an adaptive radix trie (server/stree).
when_to_use: Internal service-to-service events, fan-out and request/reply where you want replayable persistence and sub-millisecond p50 at modest rates (the test: 0.5 ms p50 at 500 msg/s with small JSON messages).
Edge, IoT or small deployments that want one static binary with no JVM and no separate controller quorum. Release builds cover Linux on many architectures, macOS, Windows and FreeBSD.
Workloads that need both queue semantics (work-queue retention, per-message ack and redelivery, shared pull consumers) and log-style replay in one system, plus KV or object storage.
Many fine-grained or hierarchical subjects consumed with wildcard filters (for example per-entity subjects), instead of a fixed set of partitioned topics.
when_not_to_use: You depend on Kafka's wire protocol or ecosystem (Connect, Kafka Streams, ksqlDB, schema registry, key-based log compaction). NATS offers a Kafka bridge connector, not API compatibility.

You need acknowledged writes to survive power loss and plan to run the defaults. JetStream acks before fsync (sync_interval 2 min). Jepsen (NATS 2.12.1, Dec 2025) lost 131,418 of 930,005 acked writes under coordinated power failure, and issues #7549, #7556, #7564 and #7567 (loss from .blk bit-flips, stream deletion from corrupt snapshots, deferred fsync, split-brain) were still open on 2026-09-26.

High-throughput partitioned ingestion: the same benchmark's burst mode showed no clear throughput win (NATS ~269-339K vs Kafka ~252-333K msg/s producer-side), and replicated or multi-partition setups were not measured at all.
Very high subject or dedup-ID cardinality on file-backed streams: per-subject and dedup indexes stay in RAM, and open issue #8485 reports OOMs or GC-driven latency when memory is capped.

integration.form: standalone server binary (tar.gz/zip/deb/rpm and the official `nats` Docker image); JetStream enabled with `-js` or a `jetstream {}` config block; the source is the Go module github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2
integration.dependencies: None at runtime (single Go binary). Go module deps: klauspost/compress (S2), minio/highwayhash, nats-io jwt/nkeys/nuid/nats.go, golang.org/x/crypto, x/sys, x/time, google/go-tpm, antithesis-sdk-go (no-op build). Apps need a NATS client with JetStream support (the benchmark used nats.go v1.52.0).
integration.min_toolchain: Prebuilt binaries need nothing. Building from source needs Go 1.26.0 (go.mod declares toolchain go1.26.8). The benchmark client was built with Go 1.25.
integration.platforms: v2.15.0 release binaries: Linux amd64/386/arm64/arm6/arm7/loong64/mips64le/ppc64le/riscv64/s390x, macOS amd64/arm64, Windows amd64/386/arm64, FreeBSD amd64. The benchmark ran linux/arm64 containers under OrbStack on an Apple M4.
integration.thread_safety: Server: a concurrent network service, so not a user concern. nats.go documents its connection as safe to use from multiple goroutines concurrently.

gotchas: Durability is opt-in. `sync_interval` defaults to 2 minutes, so an R1 stream can lose acknowledged messages on an OS crash or power loss, and the docs say even R3 can lose them under correlated failures. `sync_interval: always` fsyncs before every ack, which the docs call the slowest setting.

Shared pull consumers are partition-less, so two sequential messages on the same subject can go to different subscribers and ordering across parallel workers is lost. Use `partition()` subject mapping if you need per-key ordering.

JetStream publish is at-least-once. Exactly-once needs the `Nats-Msg-Id` header deduplicated within the stream's DuplicateWindow, plus consumer-side double ack. Messages are capped at 1 MB by default; the Object Store chunks larger objects.
nats.go PublishAsync allows 4000 in-flight acks by default and then stalls, waiting up to 200 ms by default. The docs also say Replicas=2 brings no benefit, so use R1, R3 or R5.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Redpanda (Kafka-API compatible, but it trailed Kafka in this same single-core, 500 msg/s test) when you don't need Kafka clients and care about small-message latency in one lightweight binary. Wisp beats NATS core pub/sub throughput but has no persistence, JetStream or clustering, so pick JetStream whenever you need durable, replayable streams.
verified_claims_summary: A personal benchmark (nipunnair/streaming-showdown) ran single-node, unreplicated nats:2.10-alpine JetStream (default file storage, R1) against Kafka 3.6 (cp-kafka 7.6.1, KRaft) in Docker under OrbStack on an Apple M4. Go 1.25 clients (nats.go PublishAsync plus an explicit-ack pull consumer, vs franz-go v1.21.4 at defaults) sent small JSON at 500 msg/s for 20 s after a 5 s warm-up, and HdrHistogram end-to-end latency came out at NATS p50 0.5 / p99 0.9 / p999 2.8 ms vs Kafka 7.2-7.8 / 12.7-13.5 / 14.0-19.1 ms; much of Kafka's median is plausibly franz-go's default 10 ms producer linger, which the bench never lowered, and NATS acked without fsync, so treat this as a light-load, client-default-sensitive result rather than a broker ceiling.
status_note: Actively maintained CNCF project (v2.15.0 released 2026-09-17, commits through 2026-09-25, ~20.8k stars, Apache-2.0, Trail of Bits audit April 2025), though the benchmark used the older 2.10 line and the four Jepsen durability issues filed in Nov 2025 remain open.
